why_it_matters: The SAT loves sentences where an opening phrase gets stuck on the wrong noun, and so do group chats: the caption ends up on the wrong photo.

concepts.text: The phrase before the comma describes whatever noun comes right after the comma
Fix it by putting the one doing the action right after the comma
Catch it in a new sentence by checking who or what the opening phrase is really about

misconception: An opening phrase can describe anything in the sentence, so 'Running to the bus, my backpack fell open' is a fine sentence
root_prerequisite: Spotting the subject of a sentence

boss.name: Dame Dangle-Dangle
boss.backstory: A duck in running shoes who carries a sign reading 'ANY PHRASE CAN DESCRIBE ANYONE' and insists her backpack ran to the bus.

taunt: My backpack was running. I have witnesses. They are also backpacks.
A phrase may describe whomever it pleases. That is the whole point of a phrase.
The backpack ran to the bus. I will not be taking questions.
heal: Excellent. The phrase will describe whatever it wishes. I thank you.
Quite right. Readers can simply guess who is running.
hit: This is most irregular. The backpack appears to have stopped running.
I did not authorize a doer to stand next to my comma.
lines.reformed: I have moved the runner. The backpack is relieved. I would like to join you.

cliffhanger: I heard a describing phrase can go at the END of a sentence too. Does the same rule work there? That can't be right… right?

quiz.question: In 'Running to the bus, my backpack fell open', who or what is the opening phrase describing, as written?
quiz.answer: My backpack: it is the noun right after the comma, so the sentence says the backpack was running.

quiz.question: Fix it: 'Running to the bus, my backpack fell open.' Keep the opening phrase.
quiz.answer: Running to the bus, I felt my backpack fall open. (The runner comes right after the comma.)

quiz.question: Is 'Covered in sprinkles, my sister ate the donut.' correct? Who is covered in sprinkles, as written?
quiz.answer: No. As written, my sister is covered in sprinkles. Fix: 'Covered in sprinkles, the donut was eaten by my sister.'
